panels.rights: All artworks were created by Kristóf Szabó / KristofLab, shown in the artist’s reproductions and in his own installation photographs and documentation videos. The rooms are reconstructed from the photographs and the gallery’s floor plan.
panels.controlsDesk: On a computer, walk forward and back with the up and down arrows or W and S, or with the scroll wheel. The left and right arrows turn, and A and D step sideways. Drag with the mouse to look around. Zoom with + and − or Ctrl and the scroll wheel; 0 resets. Shift makes you run. Open a work by clicking it, or with E or Enter. Page Down and Page Up go to the next and the previous work; the Next work button on the toolbar does the same as Page Down. T starts the tour, M mutes, Esc closes a panel. The keys on screen do the same when held with the mouse. The letter keys and the zoom keys work only while the 3D view is selected: click the view or Tab to it.
panels.controlsTouch: On a touch screen, walk with the stick on the left: press and hold it forward or back to walk, or to one side to step sideways; there is no need to drag. Pushed all the way, it runs. The ← and → buttons turn, with a tap or held down. Drag a finger across the view to look around. Zoom by pinching with two fingers, or with the + and − buttons. Open a work by tapping it. The buttons at the bottom start the tour, list the rooms and switch the sound on or off, and Next work goes on to the next work.

text: Kristóf Szabó aka KristofLab presents his most critical project yet, Artificial Paradise. His practice explores the relationship between nature and civilisation, wilderness and urbanisation, and man's artificially created habitat: the city and its symbol, the tower block.

Artificial Paradise takes this further: artificially created natural spaces, domesticated and industrialised nature. Visions of the future that seemed utopian a few decades ago (a new relationship between nature and man, the possibility of total control) have become everyday practice.

Controlled, industrialised nature calls into question the very definition of nature. Can we still speak of nature when vegetation is artificially created and sustained, and functions as a visual element? How does this affect ecology and our image of nature?

KristofLab uses his usual multimedia tools (installations, videos, paintings and collages) to explore the bizarre, alienating nature of the phenomenon, and to envision the possibilities encoded in its present.
textCredit: Text by Luca Cserhalmi, esthete, curator of the exhibition. The exhibition was opened by Barnabás Zemlényi-Kovács, theorist and independent curator.

behindTheScenes: The floor plan is traced from the gallery's floor plan and its overall length matches the building's outline on OpenStreetMap. Rooms are measured from 360° panorama photos: solving the camera position from the corners and the four canvases of known size gives the room's real size, the recess around the doorway and where the windows, the screen and the plant stood. Every painting hangs at its listed canvas size and measured height. The brick on the walls uses redrawn brick patterns, scaled so each course is 7.7 cm as measured in the gallery. The paintings and prints are the artist’s own reproductions, and the screens play the artist's videos with their own sound. The plant of Paradise Factory is the artist's own 3D model; the rest of the installation and the plastic river of Let it Flow are modelled from the photos. Three.js and Vite, no backend; the only sound is the videos' own, played from their screens with Web Audio.

human-as-error.heading: About the series
text: Humanity has been on Earth for only about 300,000 years, while life emerged around 3.5 billion years ago. Our species began to transform the planet more drastically around the time of the Industrial Revolution, and a large share of these processes falls within the last 70 years.

We can think of ourselves as an error with regard to natural diversity. Looking at the past century, it is no exaggeration to estimate a decline of two thirds. There have been 5 great mass extinctions in the history of the Earth so far, each reaching 75%. According to the Red List of the IUCN (International Union for Conservation of Nature), over the past 100 years roughly 27% of currently known species have become threatened or endangered with extinction: among them 25% of mammals, 13% of birds, 41% of amphibians and 33% of plants.

The settlement chosen as the subject of the series, Szentkirályszabadja near Veszprém, was a Russian military base and barracks that emptied after the change of regime. Nature has already brought its human-built structures under its rule. Working with these images, I deal conceptually with the disappearance of humans from nature. It takes only decades for nature to take back the domesticated landscape and for biodiversity to return. The depopulation of settlements is not the result of planned events; it can be put down to chance, with human activities among its causes. Error and its aesthetics hold a key place, and this is reflected in the pictures as well: chance plays a large part in my painting method, and I build up the glitched surfaces with abstracted brushwork.

In this series my aim is to rethink landscape painting. Nature reconquers what humans took from it, the “original” state returns, and we can once again admire its grandeur and strength, which also shows its power towering above civilisation. What connects most closely with my work is the aesthetic of ruins, and the love of them, in the painting of Caspar David Friedrich. A similar line of thought runs through both: in each case the dominion of nature towers above human activity. It reconquers what humans took. In Friedrich’s lifetime industrialisation completely transformed the world; today we are living through its culmination. Capitalism has turned even nature into a commodity. In Friedrich’s work the sublimity of nature can also signify a longing for an age when civilisation still lived in symbiosis with it. In my work the concept of humans subordinated to nature appears, so the built environment slowly turns into ruins, only hinting at the former “glory” of our civilisation.
human-as-error.note: English text supplied by the artist, with the Hungarian original.

landscape.heading: About the series
text: The theme of the series is the relationship between man and his environment in the light of capitalism. The harmonious fusion of the urban and the natural environment seems utopian in this context. In the existing system, the crossing of boundaries can have two extreme consequences. On the positive side, pushing boundaries can lead to progress, which can lead to development. Negatively: by crossing the boundary, we can set in motion irreversible processes with uncertain outcomes.

paradise-factory.heading: About the work
text: Paradise Factory explores new yet increasingly familiar configurations of the relationship between nature and civilization. Through rapid technological advancement and industrialization, the hierarchy between humans and nature has deepened, manifesting in altered landscapes, artificially sustained urban vegetation, and food crops grown entirely without sunlight in closed systems. The installation features a hydroponic cultivation setup alongside a repurposed monitor displaying manipulated footage of the growing process. This ambivalent assemblage simultaneously questions and reflects on emerging nature-constructs that, in an era of climate change, soil degradation, and food insecurity, may soon become the norm. At its core, the work poses a pressing question: where do we draw the line between the natural and the artificial today, and what do we even mean by "nature"?

let-it-flow.heading: About the work
text: Let it Flow is a site-specific installation that examines the disrupted material flows between humans and nature through the lens of recycling and object cultures created from waste. The work is composed partly of plastic waste collected from the River Tisza during the river-cleaning actions of the PET Kupa, and partly of plastic remnants generated within the artist’s own household.

The assemblage is built upon the duality of “flow” and “waste circulation”: the Tisza as a natural watercourse and plastic as an artificially produced yet now uncontrollable material process become layered onto one another. Waste does not disappear; instead, it searches for a new form. Through melting with a heat gun, the found objects partially lose their original function while entering a new, transitional plastic state. In this way, “useless” materials are reinterpreted as artworks.

Let it Flow is therefore not merely an installation, but a visual protocol following cycles of material circulation: a recontextualization of objects originating from pollution, in which the boundaries between natural and artificial systems become increasingly blurred.

artificial-paradise-videos.heading: About the videos
text: The two video works connected to the Artificial Paradise series explore artificially constructed natural environments and human-engineered ecosystems. One video focuses on the futuristic parks and vertical gardens of Singapore, while the other examines the vast artificial biomes of the Eden Project in Cornwall, England.

The soundscapes combine elements of nature and industrial civilisation. Artificially created nature sounds are mixed with recordings of factory noises, manipulated and played backwards, creating an unfamiliar and uncanny acoustic environment. The visual structure is fragmented through split-screen compositions, reversed footage and altered temporal sequences, disrupting the viewer's conventional perception of reality.

Together, the two videos envision a possible future in which nature no longer exists primarily as an autonomous ecological system, but rather as an environment designed, maintained and controlled by humans. The artificial paradise thus becomes both a promise of nature's preservation and an unsettling vision of its eventual disappearance.

artificial-paradise-prints.heading: About the series
text: The Artificial Paradise series explores the phenomenon of artificially constructed natural environments within contemporary urban spaces. Monumental parks, vertical gardens and architectural structures found in cities around the world – integrating nature into the urban infrastructure – appear both as attempts to reconnect with nature and as artificial substitutes for it.

The series envisions a possible future in which urbanisation, climate change and human activity increasingly displace natural environments, leaving humanity to encounter nature primarily through artificially constructed and carefully controlled ecosystems. In this context, Paradise does not necessarily represent an ideal state, but rather a paradoxical utopia: a symbol of both the preservation and the gradual loss of nature.

natural-life.heading: About the work
text: The video work Natural Life, presented as part of the Let It Flow project, depicts a small, recurring fragment of life: ferns and moss growing out of the cracks of a stone wall. The video loop captures an isolated glimpse of nature, suggesting its ability to take root and survive even within artificial and built environments. The work acts as a visual counterpoint to the plastic objects presented in the installation, made partly from plastic waste collected from the Tisza River and partly from the artist's own household waste. By juxtaposing these two material and visual worlds, the work draws attention to the contradiction between nature and the environmental pollution generated by human activity. Natural Life can thus be interpreted as a kind of pseudo-natural symbol, evoking the fragile presence of nature in an environment increasingly shaped by the materials and waste left behind by humanity.

openingSpeech.author: Barnabás Zemlényi-Kovács
openingSpeech.title: Opening speech for Kristóf Szabó's exhibition Artificial Paradise
openingSpeech.note: English text supplied by the artist, with the Hungarian original.
text: 165 years ago two men, both forty years old and knowing nothing of each other, one in France and the other in Ireland, each wrote a long study about smoke. It may sound surprising, but in my view Kristóf Szabó's exhibition can be placed somewhere in the connections between these two texts, both written around 1860 and, despite their related subject, seemingly very far apart. One of the men was John Tyndall, an Irish physicist who in 1859 began experiments to measure with laboratory instruments how effectively various gases, such as carbon dioxide, water vapour and methane, hold on to heat. Tyndall was thus the first to prove that certain components of the atmosphere, carbon dioxide above all, absorb and re-radiate a large part of the infrared radiation emitted by the Earth, and so warm the atmosphere. Tyndall's discovery is nothing other than what we now call the greenhouse effect. The Irish physicist carried out his research at the dawn of the second industrial revolution, that is, precisely when human activity began to drive up the concentration of carbon dioxide, which, through the greenhouse effect Tyndall described, led to global warming and to the climate crisis of our time.

If Tyndall's problem was that smoke, in a sense, stays, the other author's was precisely that it inevitably drifts away. In 1860 Charles Baudelaire published his study Artificial Paradises: for him the term, which also gives this exhibition its title, means the alternative wish-realities and ephemeral utopias induced by intoxicants such as hashish and opium. In this personal text, which largely reflects on his own drug use, Baudelaire circles the fundamental ambivalence of this intoxicated happiness and psychedelic fantasy world: unlike real social movements, this state can offer only a passing salvation, and once the drug wears off the user falls back into a bare reality that seems all the more desolate. In other words, only one step separates the artificial paradise from a real hell.

In Kristóf Szabó's works these two texts, written 165 years ago, are fused: his exhibition is filled with gigantic greenhouses built in response to global warming, mini-ecospheres designed to be sustainable, artificially created micro-Edens, or, as he himself calls them, “artificial paradises”. All of these are at once concrete scientific and technological answers to the climate situation, metaphors that point far beyond themselves, and utopias or wish-images of a sustainable future. And here it turns out that Baudelaire is present far beyond the title: although they are indeed more environmentally friendly than today's agricultural mass production, in Kristóf Szabó's exhibition these utopian “artificial natures”, just like Baudelaire's artificial paradises, are unmasked as fantasies whose sustainability is more than questionable, and which, as apparent answers to the crisis, partly seem to cover up the real questions.

John Tyndall did not yet use the greenhouse metaphor for greenhouse gases; it was introduced by the Swede Nils Ekholm in 1901. The artificial ecospheres Kristóf Szabó examines are built precisely on the greenhouse, which holds a certain dark irony, since they appear as a response to a climate crisis in which the whole planet has turned into an overheated global greenhouse. The greenhouse, the archetype of the artificial, humanly controlled environment, goes back to antiquity; the Romans already experimented with it. The greenhouse is an ecological paradox in which nature is the more ideal, the more artificial the conditions it is created in. Where nature is artificial, the artificial is natural. This ideal, seemingly untouched environment, which also appears in documentary footage in Kristóf Szabó's works, is made possible by an all-encompassing human control, that is, by the same logic that led to the present situation.

Baudelaire was not only one of the most influential, proto-avant-garde poets of his time but also a defining art critic and theorist of the period, one of the first to formulate the intellectual foundations of the emerging modern art. In 1863, two years after Artificial Paradises, Baudelaire wrote his essay The Painter of Modern Life, perhaps the first manifesto of modern art. “The transitory, the fugitive, the contingent make up one half of art; the other half is the eternal and the immutable,” Baudelaire writes. “[The artist] is looking for that quality which we may call modernity (…) His task is to extract from fashion whatever poetry within history it may contain, to distil the eternal from the transitory.” Despite all the crises of modernity, Baudelaire's avant-garde definition of art still sets the basic frame of art today. Kristóf Szabó, too, stands with one foot in tradition and the other in the ephemeral present; it is enough to mention his conscious dialogue with the traditional genre of the landscape. In the time of Tyndall and Baudelaire, it was artists who created artificial ideal landscapes, and the exhibition also quotes these 19th-century romantic, academic or impressionist landscape ideals. What art once produced is produced today by industry and technology, and in this situation Kristóf Szabó sees one possible task of the artist in denaturalising this synthetically produced, harmonious nature: in revealing its artificiality, in the errors, glitches and blind spots of the flawlessly staged vision, which also appear as faults in the image.

Also at the turn of the 1850s and 1860s, in 1859, a third book appeared from a third gentleman, ten years older than the other two: On the Origin of Species by Charles Darwin. Kristóf Szabó approaches the origin of species from the end of species, natural selection from artificial selection. His works claim that man is not only not the crown of creation but not even the peak of evolution; in fact, an error. Human as Error. The question is what correcting this error would mean: besides the radical transformation or abolition of capitalism, posthuman and post-anthropocentric theories argue that, if we do not want to abolish ourselves, it is precisely our human-centredness that we have to overcome in order to survive.
Our problem today is still that of Baudelaire and Tyndall: the smoke of utopia drifts away, but the smoke of dystopia stays.

A non-commercial digital exhibition that can be walked through in the browser. It documents Artificial Paradise, the exhibition of Kristóf Szabó / KristofLab at MAMŰ Gallery, Budapest (10–31 January 2025).
Netlify, Inc., 101 2nd Street, San Francisco, CA 94105, USA.

The artworks, photographs, videos and texts are In Copyright: they are protected by copyright and are not licensed for reuse.
Permission is required to reuse any part of it.
This site uses no cookies, no analytics and no tracking, and does not collect personal data itself.
One setting: the language you chose, kept in your browser’s local storage so that the site opens in it next time. It never leaves your device; clearing your browser’s site data removes it.
The site is served by Netlify. To deliver it, Netlify processes technical data such as your IP address in its server logs.
For some works the full video plays in Google Drive’s player. It is loaded only when you click its button; from then on Google receives your IP address and may set its own cookies.
Links to the artist’s website, MAMŰ, Instagram, Facebook, LinkedIn and OpenStreetMap open those sites, under their own privacy policies.

Under the GDPR you can ask any controller for access to your data, its correction or its erasure. This site holds no data about its visitors; for data held by Netlify or Google, contact them. With questions, use the Contact page. You can also turn to the Hungarian data protection authority (NAIH).

This is a pilot: the first version of the digital exhibition made with accessibility in mind. It does not claim conformance with WCAG. I worked from WCAG 2.2 and the W3C's XR Accessibility User Requirements, and this page says what was tested, what works and what does not work yet.

Automated: axe-core 4.14 through Playwright in Chromium, on the accessible version (text format) in both languages (light and dark) and on the digital exhibition in each of its states: the title screen, every panel, the sound question, the controls inside, the rooms menu, Help and the artwork viewer, also with the frame of the full video (with Google's player blocked). Result on 16 November 2026: no violations in any of the 38 states. axe could not judge the contrast of text that lies over the 3D view or a picture; I measured the contrast over the 3D view in screenshots instead (see What works).

Keyboard only: a scripted run in Chromium from page load, with Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Esc, Page Down, Page Up and T: the skip link and back, every panel, the sound question, the viewer, all 17 works, the tour, the rooms menu, the language switch, Help, the Next work button, and the letter keys with and without focus on the 3D view. All 35 steps passed. Another run checked the mouse and focus: after a click on the floor plan, the toolbar, the rooms menu, the language switch, a footer link or a Close button, the letter keys still work; while the sound question is open, the bar at the top cannot be used with the mouse or with Tab; with a panel or the viewer open, focus stays in it when the language is switched; while a panel, the viewer or the sound question is open, the browser hides the page behind it from screen readers; closing a work opened from the list of works brings the list back on that work; in a narrow window, closing a panel opened from the menu puts focus on the Menu button; and after the sound question is answered with the mouse, the 3D view has focus without the keyboard frame (58 of 58 steps).

What a screen reader is given, read in Chromium from what the browser passes to it: the names of the 3D view, the floor plan, the installation photos and the video players, the viewer's count and what its Previous and Next say, and the English titles marked as English on the Hungarian page (24 of 24 steps). Another run checks what is on screen around the 3D view, from a window of 320 × 256 pixels (a page at 400% zoom) to laptop size, with a mouse and with touch: the key under the floor plan, the first-use card, Help, the Next work button, the touch hint, the turning buttons by the stick, the artwork viewer on a phone on its side, the small layout for high zoom, the first line of the tour caption and the colours of the interface (74 of 74 steps).

Reduced motion: 18 automated checks in Chromium, with the system setting emulated and without it. With it there is no grain, no colour fringes, no pulsing and no animation in the interface, the tour jumps from stop to stop, the mouse under the walking keys does not roll its wheel and the dot that marks you on the floor plan does not swell after a jump.
Phone width: the accessible version at 375 pixels, with and without JavaScript, and the digital exhibition in Chromium's phone emulation, upright (375 × 667) and on its side (667 × 375), with touch.

Flashing: frames drawn at a fixed 60 a second and compared cell by cell. The glitch effect that marked a room change could flash up to 10 times a second when jumps followed each other quickly, so it is removed for everyone. Without it, the most measured was 2 flashes in a second, with Page Down pressed six times a second.

Not tested yet: any screen reader, Firefox and Safari, real phones and tablets, real browser zoom at 200% or more (windows of the same size in CSS pixels were checked: a laptop at 200% and a page at 400%), the Google Drive video player, and visits by people with disabilities.

The accessible version gives the whole exhibition without 3D graphics and without JavaScript: the four rooms in visiting order, the 17 works with their data and where each one hung, the texts and the credits. It is the first link on the page.

Keyboard: Tab reaches every button and link, and each shows a focus ring. Panels, the artwork viewer and the sound question take focus when they open, keep Tab inside, close with Esc and hand focus back to where you were. While one of them is open, the browser hides the page behind it from screen readers. Behind a panel or the viewer the bar at the top stays usable, so the language can still be switched; behind the sound question it is hidden too. Closing a work opened from the list of works brings the list back, with focus on the work last shown. In a narrow window, closing a panel opened from the menu puts focus on the Menu button. While the sound question is open, a click anywhere else on the screen answers it with “Without sound” and opens nothing. Switching the language while a panel or the viewer is open leaves focus in it. Page Down and Page Up go to the next and the previous work; the Next work button on the toolbar goes to the next one, one work for each press. Enter opens the work in front of you. Help, on the toolbar (in a narrow window, in the menu), shows all the controls in a panel.

When a screen reader reaches the 3D view, it says that this is the 3D view, which keys go from work to work, open a work and walk, and that all the keys are in the accessible version. While walking, it announces the room and the exhibited work currently in focus, and the floor plan's name says which room you are in. In the artwork viewer, Previous and Next go through the 17 works and say the new one with its number (“No. 3 of 17”); an installation photo is named as a photo of the work in the gallery, and the video and the Google Drive player have names. On the Hungarian page the artist's English titles are marked as English, so a screen reader that switches language reads them in an English voice. Opening a panel stops the tour, so its captions are not read over the panel.

Inside, a short card by the keys shows how to move. It goes at the first key, click or turn of the wheel, and Help can show it again; nothing is stored, so it shows on each visit. On a touch screen a hint says how to move by touch instead, and the sound question names the Sound button. A key under the floor plan says which marks are the videos and which are the other works. The tour caption says how far along the tour is (“3 / 17”).

With reduced motion switched on in your system, the digital exhibition has no grain, no colour fringes and no pulsing, the tour jumps from stop to stop, and the mouse under the walking keys and the dot that marks you on the floor plan stay still. Without the setting they move only for a moment: the wheel rolls three times, and the dot swells for 3 seconds after a jump. The loading screen is a still image for everyone.

Over the 3D view the bar at the top and the footer sit on a dark band, and the room name, the floor plan, the toolbar, the rooms menu, the keys and the captions on dark glass. In screenshots facing the brightest wall, the white brick of Room 1, I measured the bar at the top, the footer, the room name, the toolbar, the keys and the numbers on the floor plan at 5.1:1 or more, and the grey titles in the rooms menu at 4.74:1. The key under the floor plan, worked out from its colours, is 7.16:1 even over pure white. The accent colour of the interface is a light blue: worked out from its colours, it is at least 5.76:1 on the dark glass, even over pure white. No state is shown by colour alone: a pressed button on the toolbar also has a bar under it, and the room you are in is in bold in the rooms menu and on the floor plan.

On a touch screen, pressing and holding the stick walks at once, with no need to drag, and two buttons by it, ← and →, turn. On a phone on its side the artwork viewer shows the work and its text side by side. On a touch screen the buttons of the bar at the top and its menu, the toolbar, the rooms menu, the panels, the sound question and the viewer are at least 44 by 44 pixels. The footer's links are 24 pixels tall in a window up to 760 pixels wide. The title screen, the panels and the viewer can be pinch-zoomed, while the 3D view keeps its own gestures: drag to look around, pinch to zoom the view. I checked both in Chromium's phone emulation, not on a real phone.

In a very small window, such as a page zoomed to 400% (320 × 256 pixels on a 1280 × 1024 screen), the controls over the 3D view take less room: the toolbar is at the bottom, the room name and the zoom readout at the top, and the on-screen keys, the floor plan and the footer are left out; the footer's links and Help are in the menu. Nothing lies over anything else, and Tab reaches every control inside the window.

The live announcements were checked as text only. How a screen reader reads them in the digital exhibition is not known yet, nor whether it switches to an English voice for the titles marked as English on the Hungarian page.

The letter keys T, M, E, W, A, S, D and the zoom keys work only while the 3D view has focus, which is what WCAG 2.1.4 asks; a click on the view or Tab gives it focus. They cannot be switched off or changed.
The works have no descriptions of what they show, and the videos have no captions, transcripts or audio description. The accessible version gives each work's data, its place and the artist's text.
On a touch phone the 3D view of the digital exhibition cannot be used with a screen reader. The accessible version can.
By keyboard you can walk and turn left and right, but not look up or down. The floor plan can only be clicked; the rooms menu does the same by keyboard.
Walking means holding a key down. Page Down and Page Up, the Next work button, the rooms menu and the tour move you without holding anything.
The tour's captions change by themselves: after 5 seconds, or 14 at the videos with sound. The tour can be stopped (T or Esc) but not paused or slowed.

The contrast over the 3D view was measured in Chromium screenshots facing the brightest wall, not in front of every wall. The tour caption, the line that names the work in front of you, the drag hint and the touch hint, the first-use card and the zoom readout sit on the same dark glass but were not measured. Over pure white the grey titles in the rooms menu work out at 4.66:1 on the slightly darker glass (4.48:1 before), but on the row under the mouse they would fall to 3.4:1, under the 4.5:1 that WCAG asks for text of this size. The exhibition text sheets drawn on the walls of Room 1 and Room 2 were not measured.
Most labels over the 3D view and in the bar at the top are still capitals at 9 to 11 pixels, which are hard to read with low vision. The browser's zoom enlarges them.

If the browser on a laptop reports a touch screen, the digital exhibition treats the laptop as a phone: the mouse cannot look around or open works, and the on-screen keys and the footer are hidden. This is not fixed yet.

On a touch screen some links are still small. In a window wider than 760 pixels (a tablet, say) the footer's links are 13 pixels tall, and the links in the text of the panels are 17 to 20 pixels tall per line, at any width.

Esc does not close the viewer while focus is inside the Google Drive player, because the browser keeps the keys inside the player's frame: Tab or Shift+Tab, pressed until focus leaves the player, gets out of it, and then Esc works, or the Close button closes the viewer.
An audio description of the space. A view that shows what in the reconstruction was measured and what was guessed. A test with the NVDA screen reader on Windows.
If something does not work, please tell {link} by e-mail.
